1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
18

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the bearing face 26 bears on the exposed face 38, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
54	
55	Handles
56	
57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
58	
59	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
64	
65	Method of use
66	
67	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
68

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the bearing face 26 bears on the exposed face 38, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is spent on loosening the hold and driving the body along the surface, rather than being delivered into the surface as the working output of the tool. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto the covering element 36. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Line work only; the only characters on the sheet are the listed numerals and their leaders, with the view legend FIG. 1 below the drawing, clear of all line work.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile, a flat rectangular panel seen in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is a plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round the underside of the slab, the band alone touching the tile. Two plain closed housings stand on the top face of the slab, one to the left and one to the right of it, and a grip stands above the slab between them. Slab, band, housings and grip are shown schematically.

Every body on the sheet is a plain solid in simple outline. Where two faces of a body meet, they meet along one shared edge that is drawn once and serves both faces. No face carries hatching, shading, texture, seams, fasteners, controls or any other detail, and no rim, ledge, chamfer or second boundary is drawn just inside the edges of a face.

The band stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the upper face of the tile with no gap between them.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, that is the slab together with its band, its housings and its grip. Identified on the outline bounding the left-hand side face of the slab, well below the grip.
- The base 12 is the slab, its top face visible where no housing stands on it. Identified well inside that visible top face, clear of the housings and of the grip.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand housing. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand housing. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band under the slab. Identified well inside the front surface of the band, the surface that faces the viewer between the underside of the slab and the tile.

That shape is a depiction convention for this sheet only, and the place at which the grip meets the machine is shown schematically, no number of connections, attachment location or attachment formation being shown. Identified on the bar of the grip, above the slab, not in the open area the ring encloses.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to the right of the machine, clear of the machine.

- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to the right of the machine, clear of the machine.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto the covering element 36. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Line work only; the only characters on the sheet are the listed numerals and their leaders, with the view legend FIG. 1 below the drawing, clear of all line work.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile, a flat rectangular panel seen in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is a plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round the underside of the slab, the band alone touching the tile. Two plain closed housings stand on the top face of the slab, one to the left and one to the right of it, and a grip stands above the slab between them. Slab, band, housings and grip are shown schematically.

Every body on the sheet is a plain solid in simple outline. Where two faces of a body meet, they meet along one shared edge that is drawn once and serves both faces. No face carries hatching, shading, texture, seams, fasteners, controls or any other detail, and no rim, ledge, chamfer or second boundary is drawn just inside the edges of a face.

The band stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the upper face of the tile with no gap between them.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab with its band, housings and grip. Identified on the outline bounding the left-hand side face of the slab, well below the grip.
- The base 12 is the slab, its top face visible where no housing stands on it. Identified well inside that visible top face, clear of the housings and of the grip.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand housing. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand housing. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band under the slab. Identified well inside the front surface of the band, which faces the viewer between the underside of the slab and the tile.
- The handle 44 is the grip carried on the machine above the slab and clear of the housings, drawn as a closed ring shape enclosing an open area, the bar forming that ring having its own width. That shape is a depiction convention for this sheet only, and the place at which the grip meets the machine is shown schematically, no attachment formation being shown. Identified on the bar of the grip, above the slab, not in the open area the ring encloses.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to the right of the machine, clear of the machine.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. VIBRATION DEVICE FOR BEDDING COVERING ELEMENTS, HELD BY A SUSTAINED PRESSURE DIFFERENTIAL ACROSS A RIGID LOW-FRICTION PERIMETER
Not applicable.
Not applicable.
The present disclosure relates to power tools for installing tiles and other covering elements, whether guided by hand or drawn across the work by a flexible pulling element, and more particularly to a vibration device that transmits mechanical vibration into a covering element that has been placed on a bed of thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material, in order to release trapped air, distribute the bonding material and improve the contact between the covering element and the bonding material.
A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force being required from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

content.text: I revised only the four figure briefs the reviewer failed; the application text, claims, numeral table, and FIG. 2 are untouched.

input.summary: Repaired the four drawing specifications the reviewer failed (FIG. 1, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, FIG. 5) and left every other file, including the passing FIG. 2, the patent text, the claims, and the numeral table, exactly as they were. Each of the reported semantic failures was a conflict between the rendered sheet and an absolute prohibition I had written into the brief, or a genuine rendering artifact, so the fix was in the briefs, never in the invention. FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 previously carried the rule "every edge is one single line, and no line runs parallel and close to another", which no perspective view of a solid body can satisfy: a slab, a band and a tile drawn in perspective necessarily show thickness edges that run parallel and close. The reviewer's "doubled line" findings on the slab, the band, the tile and the grip were all quotations of that impossible rule. The briefs now describe what a perspective line drawing of these bodies actually contains, faces meeting along one shared edge drawn once, while forbidding what was genuinely wrong: a second boundary, rim, ledge or chamfer drawn just inside the edges of a face, and any texture, seam, fastener or control on a face. The handle is now described as a closed ring whose bar has its own width, which is what a grip looks like, instead of the single unclosed contour the old brief demanded. FIG. 5 lost its "one continuous outer silhouette" requirement, which the renderer had answered with two stepped slab plates; its machine is now one plain rectangular body on a band, with the unnumbered housings dropped so there is less for the renderer to garble, and the cord is one slack curved path that lies wholly to the left of the machine and nowhere crosses it, which cures the "cord crosses the silhouette" finding. FIG. 3 failed because the ring was rendered subdivided into four closed regions; the brief now forbids diagonal or mitre lines at the corners and any line crossing the band, so the ring reads as one continuous surface between two concentric rectangles. FIG. 4 failed on an interrupted, partly unhatched top band and a third vertical line; the column is now placed midway across the sheet with open paper on both sides, each band runs the full width with hatching continuous from side to side including directly beneath the column, and the brittle assertion that the column's two side lines were the only vertical lines on the sheet is gone. All five briefs are now within the 2800 character limit. Numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 on FIG. 1; 16, 24 on FIG. 3; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 on FIG. 4; 10, 24, 36, 46 on FIG. 5. Every numeral in draft/numerals.md still appears on at least one sheet and every numeral on a sheet is in the table. One thing I could not do: I would have preferred to rename the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 files, but file renaming and deletion are not permitted to me in this workspace, so the existing filenames and figure titles are preserved and the briefs were written to remain accurate under those titles. The FIG. 5 leader for 38 in FIG. 4 moved from the right of the column to the left, and 36 from the left to the right, because the column now sits in the middle; both endpoints remain on the parts named in the numeral table.
reasoning: The reviewer's FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 findings all quoted one sentence I had written: 'every edge is one single line, and no line runs parallel and close to another'. That sentence cannot be satisfied by a perspective view of any solid with thickness, so the sheets could never pass while it stood. I removed it and replaced it with the constraint that actually expresses the defect: faces meet along one shared edge drawn once, and no second boundary, rim, ledge or chamfer is drawn just inside the edges of a face. The doubled slab and tile edges the reviewer saw were legitimate thickness; the thin stripe inside the band's front surface was not, and the new wording forbids exactly that.

The handle findings were the same problem in miniature. My brief demanded 'one single closed outline', and the renderer drew a grip with wall thickness and a strap, which is what a grip looks like. Rather than fight it, the brief now says the handle is drawn as a closed ring whose bar has its own width, and keeps the part that matters for the patent: the ring shape and the meeting place with the machine are a depiction convention shown schematically, with no attachment formation shown. Nothing about the handle's shape or attachment has been added to the specification or claims, because the disclosure says only that the device may include one or more handles used for guiding.

FIG. 5's 'separate slab plates at two levels with an intervening step' was real broken geometry, not a wording conflict. I cut the sheet's body count: the machine is now one plain rectangular body on a band, and the two housings, which carry no numeral on that sheet, are gone. Fewer bodies means fewer chances for the renderer to invent a step. The brief description of FIG. 5 in draft/07-drawings.md already said the vibration device and the perimeter member are shown schematically, so no text change was needed to support the simplification.

The cord finding was that it crossed the machine's silhouette instead of terminating at it. The brief now states the cord begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine and lies wholly to the left, nowhere passing across the machine. I also dropped 'of even thickness', which had invited the renderer to outline a tube; it is now simply one slack curved path in the manner of a loose cord, targeted as a path.

FIG. 3's failure, four closed rectangular regions where the spec required two, is the classic mitre artifact: a renderer closes a ring's corners with diagonals and produces four trapezoids. Restating 'exactly two closed lines' had already failed once, so instead of repeating the count I named the artifact and forbade it: plain square corners, no diagonal or mitre line at any corner, no line crossing the band at any place, so the band is not divided into separate sides or any other closed region.

FIG. 4 had two findings, and one of them was caused by my own layout. The column stood in the left-hand part of the sheet directly over the left end of the covering element band, and the renderer responded by breaking and part-unhatching that band. Moving the column to the middle of the width gives open paper on both sides and lets each band run the full width uninterrupted, which the brief now states explicitly, including that the hatching continues directly beneath the column. I also deleted the assertion that the column's two side lines were the only vertical lines on the sheet, because a band closed at its ends produces further verticals and the assertion was an unnecessary trap; the sheet's meaning does not depend on a vertical line count.
I did not touch FIG. 2. It passed, and the request is to preserve everything a gate has not shown to be wrong.

I made no change to the specification, the claims, the numeral table, or the brief description of the drawings. Nothing in the repairs widened or narrowed a structure: every part still appears on the same sheet with the same numeral and the same canonical name, and the only substantive drawing content removed anywhere is the two unnumbered housings on FIG. 5, which were never relied on by the text. This keeps the rule that the sources govern the text, the text governs the briefs, and the briefs govern the sheets, with no traffic in the other direction.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the feature combination that carries it clear of the art: a rigid, low-friction perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously, and an extraction rate high enough to hold the chamber below atmosphere in spite of that inflow, with the whole vibration path rigid and the bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Nothing in this turn's repairs bears on that.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: simplified the machine to one plain rectangular body on a band, removing the unnumbered housings and the 'one continuous outer silhouette' requirement that the renderer answered with stepped plates; applied the same shared-edge and no-second-boundary wording as FIG. 1; specified that the flexible pulling element 46 is one slack curved path beginning where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, lying wholly to the left and nowhere passing across the machine; dropped 'of even thickness' so the cord is targeted as a path.

figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: replaced the bare 'exactly two closed lines' count with a positive description of one rectangle inside another sharing a common centre, and forbade the artifact that caused the failure, namely diagonal or mitre lines at the corners and any line crossing the band, so the band reads as one continuous surface and not as four closed regions.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the review raised no citation or claim issue and the repairs were confined to drawing specifications. The Background still addresses all five listed references and the independent claims still stand on the same distinguishing combination. DE-202021002652-U1 teaches a hand-held tile lifting and laying device whose vibrated shafts carry suction cups formed by rubber-elastic aprons and evacuated by a pump; the claimed perimeter member is rigid, of low-friction material, free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and deliberately does not seal, so the compliant cup wall that damps vibration in that device is absent from the claimed path. **View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted. **Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile, a flat rectangular panel seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the left.

The machine is shown schematically as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile. No housing, grip or other part is drawn on it.

Every body on the sheet is a plain solid in simple outline. Where two faces of a body meet, they meet along one shared edge that is drawn once and serves both faces. The band stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the upper face of the tile with no gap between them.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path, in the manner of a loose cord. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place being shown schematically with no attachment formation shown, and runs away to the left, sagging gently over the open expanse of tile and ending free well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area. It lies wholly to the left of the machine and nowhere passes across the machine.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, drawn here as the rectangular body with its band, the omitted parts not being shown. - The perimeter member 24 is the band under the rectangular body. Identified well inside the front surface of the band, which faces the viewer between the underside of the rectangular body and the tile.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is that one slack curved path. Identified on the path where it runs over the open expanse of tile, clear of the machine.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to the left of the machine, clear of the machine and of the flexible pulling element 46.

input.summary: Fixed the two verified findings, both confined to the FIG. 5 package, and touched nothing else. First, the pulling element sentence in the FIG. 5 brief told the renderer to start the cord at the left-hand side of the machine while also disclaiming any attachment location, which cannot both be executed. The disclaimer now covers only the attachment formation, matching how the FIG. 1 handle entry is written, so the location is stated once and the hardware is refused once. Second, FIG. 5 draws the machine without the two housings, and nothing told the reader that the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism were merely left off, with the result that numeral 10 appeared to designate a smaller assembly than on FIG. 1. The View line of the FIG. 5 brief now states that the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted, the callout for 10 defines it as the whole machine drawn here as the rectangular body with its band with those two parts omitted, and the FIG. 5 sentence in the Brief Description of the Drawings now carries "the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being omitted for clarity", which is the same treatment already given to FIG. 2. Numeral 10 therefore means the same assembly on both sheets. No claim, no numeral definition, no detailed description sentence and no disclosed embodiment changed, and no technical matter was added: the omission statement is a drawing convention, and the cord still shows no attachment hardware, which is all the disclosure supports since it says only that a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. The added sentences pushed the FIG. 5 brief over the 2800 character limit, so I recovered the space by tightening three sentences that carried no geometry, using wording already used in the FIG. 1 brief for the same shared-edge and no-second-boundary rules. All five briefs now measure 2796, 2799, 2531, 2788 and 2797 characters. The numeral table and every numeral-to-sheet assignment are untouched: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 on FIG. 1; 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36 on FIG. 2; 16, 24 on FIG. 3; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 on FIG. 4; 10, 24, 36, 46 on FIG. 5.
reasoning: The cord finding was a genuine contradiction of my own making. A drawn line that meets the left-hand side of a body necessarily shows where it meets, so disclaiming the location while specifying it left the renderer no executable instruction. Deleting the location disclaimer and keeping the formation disclaimer preserves exactly what the disclosure supports, a flexible pulling element connected to the device with no hardware described, while giving the renderer one unambiguous starting point.

The numeral 10 finding is a labelling defect, not a support defect, so I fixed it with statements about the drawing rather than by adding housings to FIG. 5 or by narrowing what 10 means. Adding the two housings back would have reintroduced the body count that produced the stepped-plate rendering artifact on this sheet in the previous round; stating the omission costs nothing and is the convention the application already uses for FIG. 2, where the vibration motor and the handle are omitted for clarity.

The sheet shows four hatched bodies and nothing else: one upright column, the perimeter member 24, shown schematically as one hatched body, and three horizontal bands lying one above another beneath it.

The three bands are stacked one on another in the lower part of the drawing area. Its two side lines run straight down from the upper limit of the drawing area to one horizontal line closing the column below, the hatching running whole between them. content.text: The convention declaration is now applied to every drawn body on FIGS. 1, 4 and 5, with no change to the application text.

input.summary: Fixed the single finding: the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate were given drawn outlines on FIGS. 1, 4 and 5 while the words "shown schematically" were reserved for the other bodies on those same sheets. The three briefs now declare the convention for every body they draw, in the same form FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 already used. FIG. 1 reads "Slab, band, housings, grip and tile are shown schematically, the plain rectangular tile form being a depiction convention for this sheet only." FIG. 4 reads "one upright column, the perimeter member 24, and three horizontal bands lying one above another beneath it, all four bodies shown schematically, the plain rectangular band forms being a depiction convention for this sheet only", which covers the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate as well as the perimeter member. FIG. 5 reads "The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, the plain rectangular forms being a depiction convention for this sheet only." I also deleted the phrase "a flat rectangular panel seen in perspective" from the tile sentence in FIGS. 1 and 5, so the tile's form is now asserted once, inside the declared convention, rather than twice. The convention is confined to the figure briefs: the claims, the Detailed Description, the Brief Description of the Drawings and the numeral table are untouched, and all three parts remain shape-neutral in the application text, as the disclosure names them without describing their form. The added declarations pushed FIGS. 1, 4 and 5 over the 2800 character limit, so I recovered the room from wording that carried no geometry: the "clear of all line work" tail on the view legend sentence, the redundant "just" in the no-second-boundary rule, and a few restatements such as "between the underside of the slab and the tile" for the band's front surface, which now reads "beneath the slab". Two endpoint modifiers went with them, "clear of its ends" on the bearing face 26 leader in FIG. 4 and "to the left of the machine" on the covering element 36 leader in FIG. 5, both of which were placement fussiness rather than part identification; each endpoint still names one part unambiguously. The five briefs now measure 2798, 2799, 2531, 2793 and 2789 characters. Numeral assignments are unchanged: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 on FIG. 1; 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36 on FIG. 2; 16, 24 on FIG. 3; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 on FIG. 4; 10, 24, 36, 46 on FIG. 5.
reasoning: The defect was in the declaration, not the depiction, so the fix went only into the figure briefs. Putting an example-form sentence about the tile, the bonding bed or the substrate into the specification would have added matter the disclosure does not contain: it names these three parts and says nothing about their form. Keeping the convention inside the briefs leaves the application text shape-neutral, which is what the claims and description already are.

FIG. 4 needed the declaration to reach all four bodies, not just the perimeter member, because the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate are the three bands whose full-width rectangular form the brief fixes. Wording it as 'all four bodies shown schematically' covers the column and the three bands in one clause and costs fewer characters than declaring each band separately.

Removing 'a flat rectangular panel seen in perspective' from FIGS. 1 and 5 does double duty: it takes out a second, undeclared assertion of the tile's shape, and it frees characters. The tile is still drawn as a plain tile in perspective, and its rectangular form is now stated once, inside the sentence that declares it a convention for that sheet.

The character ceiling forced choices about what to cut, and I cut only wording that constrained nothing a check can measure. input.summary: Fixed the single finding. The FIG. 5 brief fixes the viewpoint as a perspective view from above and to the front left, which shows the front face and the left-hand side face of the machine and turns the right-hand side face away, yet the callout for numeral 10 directed the leader to the outline bounding the right-hand side face. That endpoint now reads "Identified on the outline bounding the front face of the rectangular body, clear of the band and remote from the flexible pulling element 46." The front face is visible from the stated viewpoint, so the instruction is executable; "clear of the band" keeps the endpoint off the perimeter member 24, which is labelled separately on the same sheet, and "remote from the flexible pulling element 46" keeps it away from the corner where the cord leaves the machine on the left, without naming an exact position along the outline. Numeral 10 still designates the whole machine, matching FIG. 1, and it is still identified on the machine's outline rather than inside a face, which is what distinguishes it from 12 on FIG. 1 and from 24 on this sheet. Nothing else changed. No claim, no sentence of the Detailed Description, no line of the Brief Description of the Drawings, no numeral definition and no other figure brief was touched, and the drawn geometry of FIG. 5 is unchanged: the same plain body on a band, standing on the right-hand part of the tile, with the pulling element running off to the left. The edit is the same length as the text it replaced, so all five briefs remain within the 2800 character limit at 2798, 2799, 2531, 2793 and 2788 characters, and the numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 on FIG. 1; 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36 on FIG. 2; 16, 24 on FIG. 3; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 on FIG. 4; 10, 24, 36, 46 on FIG. 5.
reasoning: The contradiction was between two lines of the same brief, so I fixed the endpoint rather than the viewpoint. Changing the viewpoint would have broken the deliberate parallel with FIG. 1, which uses the identical view and is the sheet FIG. 5 is meant to be read against, and would have forced a rewrite of geometry that no check has faulted.

I chose the front face over the left-hand side face because the cord leaves the machine on the left. Putting the leader for 10 on the left-hand outline would have crowded the endpoint against the flexible pulling element 46 and its own leader, trading one endpoint defect for another.

The qualifier is 'remote from the flexible pulling element 46' rather than a fraction, midpoint or named corner of the front outline. It does the separating work that is actually needed, keeping the endpoint away from the side where the cord attaches, without inventing a placement coordinate that the disclosure does not ground.

Numeral 10 stays on the outline, not inside a face. That is the convention this figure set uses to distinguish the whole machine from its parts: 10 on the silhouette, 12 inside the slab's top face on FIG. 1, 24 inside the band's front surface here. Moving 10 into a face would have made it compete with 24 on the same sheet.

I made no change to the application text, because the defect never reached it. The description says a flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 and says nothing about which face of the device a leader touches.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn. The review recorded source fidelity, formalities, claim and numeral consistency as otherwise clean and raised nothing about the claims or the Background, and the finding was a leader endpoint internal to one figure brief, so no claim or citation text was touched. Claim 1 still stands on the combination the folder does not teach: a rigid perimeter member of low-friction material that is not asked to seal, a clearance along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, and an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure in spite of that inflow, with every member of the vibration path rigid and the bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 puts rubber-elastic suction cup aprons in the vibration path; US-11408462-B2 forms its peripheral wall from elastic partitions and adds a rigid frame only to stop them being drawn inward; US-10001245-B2 gives up vacuum coupling and switches to a blower air cushion in order to move, so it never holds and slides at once; US-4934475-A uses a seal member and spends its vibration on reducing the adhering force and driving the body along the wall rather than delivering it into the work; US-11247858-B2 lifts sheet articles clear on a perforated suction plate and cleans by suction. Moving a leader endpoint from a hidden face to a visible one does not touch that analysis.

input.summary: Fixed the single finding by extending the existing "shown schematically" recitals in draft/07-drawings.md so that they reach every element the figure briefs already draw under a declared depiction convention. FIG. 1 now ends "the handle, the vibration motor, the air-extraction mechanism, the base, the perimeter member and the covering element being shown schematically." FIG. 2 now ends "and the air-extraction mechanism, the base, the perimeter member, the covering element and the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber being shown schematically." FIG. 4 now ends "the perimeter member, the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate being shown schematically." FIG. 5 now ends "and the vibration device, the perimeter member and the covering element being shown schematically." FIG. 3 was left alone, because its only schematically drawn body, the perimeter member, was already declared in both places. Nothing was added but the names of parts that already appear in the numeral table and in these same sentences: no shape, no proportion, no count, no "by way of example" phrase, no optional-outline language, and no new embodiment. The figure briefs, the claims, the Detailed Description, the Abstract and the numeral table are untouched, so the application text remains shape-neutral about the tile, the bonding bed and the substrate, which is all the disclosure supports, since it names them without describing their form. All five briefs remain within the character limit at 2798, 2799, 2531, 2793 and 2788 characters, and the numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 on FIG. 1; 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36 on FIG. 2; 16, 24 on FIG. 3; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 on FIG. 4; 10, 24, 36, 46 on FIG. 5.
reasoning: The gap was between two files that must agree: the briefs declared the tile, the bonding bed and the substrate to be generic outlines, and the Brief Description of the Drawings enumerated schematic elements per figure without naming them. Extending the recital closes the gap in the direction that adds nothing, since 'shown schematically' is a disclaimer of appearance, not an assertion about structure.

I fixed the text rather than the briefs because the briefs are right: the disclosure names the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate and says nothing about their form, so any drawn outline for them is a rendering convention and must be declared as one. Deleting the declarations from the briefs would have left the drawn rectangles undisclaimed, which is the worse of the two directions.

FIG. 3 got no edit. Its brief draws only the perimeter member, already declared schematic in both the brief and the Brief Description, so touching that sentence would have been change for its own sake.

The recitals name parts and stop there. I did not write that the tile is rectangular, that the bands are uniform, or that other forms may be used, because each of those would put appearance into the application text and would be matter the disclosure does not contain.

No claim, description sentence, numeral definition or figure brief changed, so nothing needed resynchronizing beyond the four sentences themselves. The numerals for these parts, 36, 40 and 42, already appear in the Detailed Description and in the numeral table with the same names used in the new recitals.
